In @sec-13-attention, cross-attention removed the fixed-state bottleneck by connecting
the decoder to every encoder state through content-dependent weights, and scaled dot
products turned query–key comparison into matrix multiplication. Yet the serial nature
of recurrence remained.

Queries, keys, and values require neither two separate sequences nor a recurrent state.
If a sequence queries itself, every token can pool context from every position, its own
included, in one parallel operation.

That departure is the central idea of the
[*Transformer*](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/hash/3f5ee243547dee91fbd053c1c4a845aa-Abstract.html).
Abandoning recurrence, however, raises three problems: the model has no built-in
representation of token order, a single attention distribution must combine several
relationships at once, and stacking unconstrained routing layers destabilizes deep
optimization. This chapter constructs the Transformer by addressing each problem from
first principles, then trains a deliberately small causal Transformer on the book-corpus
benchmark from @sec-10-sequences-rnn.

## Self-attention: when a sequence queries itself {#let-the-sequence-query-itself}

With the scaled dot-product operator established, self-attention alters only the origin
of the three inputs: rather than coming from two distinct sequences (such as an encoder
and a decoder), all three come from the same sequence.

Consider a sentence containing the words *bank*, *river*, and *boats*. An effective
representation of *bank* should route information from *river* and *boats*, while
another occurrence, flanked by *loan* and *interest*, must integrate different context.
@sec-13-attention routed context between two sequences and reduced the score to scaled
dot products. Here each token uses that operator to query the surrounding tokens of its
own sequence.

The three operational roles remain: a query specifies what information is sought, a key
provides the features used for matching, and a value carries the content to be pooled.

Let a batch of token representations be

$$
\matr{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times n \times d},
$$

where $B$ is the batch size, $n$ is the sequence length, and $d$ is the model dimension.
Learned linear projections produce

$$
\matr{Q}=\matr{X}\matr{W}_Q,\qquad \matr{K}=\matr{X}\matr{W}_K,\qquad \matr{V}=\matr{X}\matr{W}_V,
$$

with $\matr{W}_Q,\matr{W}_K,\matr{W}_V\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$. Scaled dot-product
attention is

$$
\operatorname{Attention}(\matr{Q},\matr{K},\matr{V})
=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{\matr{Q}\matr{K}^\top}{\sqrt d}\right)\matr{V}.
$$

For a single sequence, $\matr{Q}\matr{K}^\top$ has shape $n\times n$. Row $i$ contains the
compatibility
scores from query position $i$ to every key position $j$. A row-wise softmax normalizes
each row into a probability distribution, and multiplying by $\matr{V}$ computes a weighted
combination of values for each query:

$$
(n,d)(d,n)\to(n,n),\qquad (n,n)(n,d)\to(n,d).
$$

@fig-self-attention-read traces one query, *bank*, across the four-token sequence
*bank by the river*: the same sequence supplies the queries, keys, and values, and the
query's row of the $n\times n$ attention matrix gives the weights on the rows of $\matr{V}$.

Self-attention shares its projections across positions, as an RNN shares its transition
across time (@sec-10-sequences-rnn): the weights in an attention row depend on content, and
the comparison rule that computes them is the same for every query–key pair.

The kernel smoother of @sec-12-kernel-regression compared a query and key through a
fixed distance metric and a single bandwidth. Here, training optimizes the $d\times d$
matrix $\matr{W}_Q\matr{W}_K^\top$, determining how features of the querying token
interact with features of the token being read. Because $\matr{W}_Q$ and $\matr{W}_K$ are

### Permutation equivariance without positional signals or masks {#the-position-debt}

Consider first self-attention in the absence of positional encodings or attention masks.
Permuting the input tokens permutes the output representations in the same way. (A
causal mask breaks this symmetry by assigning distinct visible prefixes to different
positions.)

Let $\matr{P}$ be an $n\times n$ permutation matrix, so that $\matr{P}\matr{X}$ reorders
the input tokens. Then

$$
\matr{Q}'=\matr{P}\matr{Q},\quad \matr{K}'=\matr{P}\matr{K},\quad \matr{V}'=\matr{P}\matr{V},
$$

and therefore

$$
\matr{Q}'\matr{K}'^\top=\matr{P}(\matr{Q}\matr{K}^\top)\matr{P}^\top.
$$

Writing $\matr{S}=\matr{Q}\matr{K}^\top/\sqrt d$, we have
$\matr{S}'=\matr{P}\matr{S}\matr{P}^\top$. Because row-wise softmax operates
along each row independently, it commutes with simultaneous row and column permutations:

$$
\operatorname{softmax}(\matr{P}\matr{S}\matr{P}^\top) =\matr{P}\operatorname{softmax}(\matr{S})\matr{P}^\top.
$$

With $\operatorname{SA}$ denoting the self-attention operator, combining these steps yields

$$
\operatorname{SA}(\matr{P}\matr{X})
=\matr{P}\operatorname{SA}(\matr{X}).
$$

Self-attention is therefore *permutation equivariant*: permuting the inputs induces
the same permutation on the outputs. It is not permutation invariant, as reordering the
input tokens permutes the output rows rather than leaving the output matrix unchanged.
However, without an external positional signal, the operator has no mechanism for
distinguishing “first” from “fifth.” Any pooling that treats all positions
symmetrically (such as mean-pooling) is therefore permutation *invariant* and reduces
the sequence to an unordered multiset.

In @sec-08-cnn, convolution had locality by construction: a convolutional filter
encodes neighborhood relationships because its kernel weights are tied to fixed relative
offsets. Global attention discards this locality bias. Without positional encodings or
structured masking, it has no intrinsic notion of sequence order.

## Positional encoding: a bank of clocks {#position-as-a-bank-of-clocks}

The simplest additive code repeats $i/(n-1)$ across every coordinate. While it supplies
order, every position vector lies along the same ray, differing only in magnitude rather
than direction. A binary code provides richer directional variation, yet adjacent
integers can differ across multiple bits, yielding poor metric locality. These are not
impossible designs. Rather, they provide weak inductive biases for a model that must
reason about relative shifts and distances.

Sinusoidal encoding equips every position with a bank of harmonic clocks. For an even
model dimension $d$ and frequency indices $j\in\{0,\dots,d/2-1\}$, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{PE}(i,2j)
&=\sin\left(i\,10000^{-2j/d}\right),\\
\operatorname{PE}(i,2j+1)
&=\cos\left(i\,10000^{-2j/d}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Small $j$ yields a fast-turning clock, and large $j$ yields a slow one. Every sine
coordinate is paired with a cosine at the same frequency. The model receives

$$
\vect{z}_i=\sqrt d\,\vect{e}_i+\operatorname{PE}(i),
$$

where $\vect{e}_i$ is the token embedding. With token embeddings initialized at coordinate standard
deviation $1/\sqrt d$ (as in the [book-corpus experiment](#the-book-reads-itself-again)
below), scaling by $\sqrt d$ gives unit-variance coordinates, so the embedding's norm,
about $\sqrt d$, is comparable to the positional vector's $\sqrt{d/2}$.

Pairing sine and cosine expresses relative shifts as linear rotations. For an angular
frequency $\omega$, advancing position $i$ by an offset $\delta$ is an exact planar
rotation:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\sin((i+\delta)\omega)\\
\cos((i+\delta)\omega)
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(\delta\omega)&\sin(\delta\omega)\\
-\sin(\delta\omega)&\cos(\delta\omega)
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\sin(i\omega)\\
\cos(i\omega)
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The transformation matrix depends only on the offset $\delta$, not on the absolute
index $i$. This gives linear layers a convenient form for representing relative
displacement. However, this is a property of the sinusoidal code itself, not a guarantee
that unconstrained learned projections $\matr{W}_Q$ and $\matr{W}_K$ will preserve or
exploit it.

In @fig-position-clocks, the four clocks of a width-8 code illustrate how a single step
turns dial $j$ by a constant angle $\omega_j$ regardless of starting position. At
$i=44$, the fastest clock ($j=0$) has completed approximately seven full revolutions and
nearly returned to its orientation at $i=0$, while the slower clocks still distinguish
the two positions.

## Rotate the queries and keys

Instead of adding positional vectors to token embeddings, an alternative is to rotate
the projected queries and keys directly. Letting $R_i$ be a block-diagonal rotation with
angles proportional to $i$, define $\widetilde{\vect{q}}_i=R_i\vect{q}_i$ and
$\widetilde{\vect{k}}_j=R_j\vect{k}_j$. Their compatibility score becomes

$$
\widetilde{\vect{q}}_i^\top\widetilde{\vect{k}}_j
=\vect{q}_i^\top R_i^\top R_j\vect{k}_j
=\vect{q}_i^\top R_{j-i}\vect{k}_j,
$$

where the final equality follows because transposition inverts each orthogonal planar
block ($R_i^\top=R_{-i}$), isolating the relative offset $j-i$. This formulation is
[**rotary positional embedding (RoPE)**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864). Semantic
content enters through $\vect{q}_i$ and $\vect{k}_j$, while RoPE injects relative
position directly into their geometric comparison.
:::

## Multi-head attention: routing across parallel subspaces {#one-routing-operation-many-heads}

A single attention distribution forces a compromise among competing retrieval criteria.
Multi-head attention runs several smaller routing systems in parallel, each operating on
its own linear projection of the sequence representations. Let the number of heads $N_h$
divide the model dimension $d$, with per-head width $D_h=d/N_h$. For each head $h$,

$$
\matr{Q}_h=\matr{X}\matr{W}_Q^{(h)},\quad \matr{K}_h=\matr{X}\matr{W}_K^{(h)},\quad \matr{V}_h=\matr{X}\matr{W}_V^{(h)},
$$

where
$\matr{W}_Q^{(h)},\matr{W}_K^{(h)},\matr{W}_V^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times D_h}$. The head
output is

$$
\matr{O}_h=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(
\frac{\matr{Q}_h\matr{K}_h^\top}{\sqrt{D_h}}+\matr{M} \right)\matr{V}_h,
$$

where $\matr{M}$ is the visibility mask defined below ($\matr{M}=0$ for unmasked attention).

The complete operation concatenates the head representations and projects them back to
model width:

$$
\operatorname{MHA}(\matr{X}) =\operatorname{Concat}(\matr{O}_1,\ldots,\matr{O}_{N_h})\matr{W}_O, \qquad \matr{W}_O\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}.
$$

Tensor shapes provide the clearest operational guide:

$$
(B,n,d)
\to(B,N_h,n,D_h)
\to(B,N_h,n,n)
\to(B,N_h,n,D_h)
\to(B,n,d).
$$

Scaling uses $\sqrt{D_h}$ rather than $\sqrt d$ because each head's dot product sums
over $D_h$ coordinates, and the variance argument of @sec-13-attention applies to that
sum. With fixed $d$, splitting into multiple heads does not increase parameter count: the
projection matrices $\matr{W}_Q$, $\matr{W}_K$, $\matr{W}_V$, and $\matr{W}_O$ together
contain $4d^2$ parameters regardless of $N_h$. Heads partition the model dimension rather
than duplicating it.

### The mask is part of the model

In @sec-11-encoder-decoder, masking specified which sequence positions were invalid.
Here, the mask enforces causality: position $i$ may attend to tokens at earlier and
current positions $j\le i$, but must not attend to future tokens $j>i$. Because rows
correspond to queries and columns to keys, the forbidden region forms a strict upper
triangle. We set

$$
\matr{M}_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
0,&j\le i,\\
-\infty,&j>i
\end{cases}
$$

*before* softmax. Zeroing forbidden probabilities after softmax would leave the
surviving distribution unnormalized.
<!-- print 2026-10-09, author-approved: adding minus infinity before softmax equals zeroing and renormalizing, so each row is the unmasked row conditioned on j <= i (the top-k and nucleus link is made where those samplers appear, in the practice bridge below) -->
Adding $-\infty$ prior to exponentiation is algebraically equivalent to setting
forbidden probabilities to zero and renormalizing the remaining probabilities by their
sum. Each row becomes the unmasked distribution conditioned on the causal event
$j\le i$. Masking every key in a row is ill-defined, as softmax over all $-\infty$
yields `NaN`. In a causal mask, the main diagonal remains visible: the representation at
position $i$ may attend to token $i$ while predicting token $i+1$.

import torch
from torch import nn
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [1]
class CausalMultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width: int, heads: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        if width % heads != 0:
            raise ValueError("width must be divisible by heads")
        self.heads = heads
        self.head_width = width // heads
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(width, 3 * width)
        self.project = nn.Linear(width, width)
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(self.qkv.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.qkv.bias)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, return_weights: bool = False):
        batch, length, width = x.shape
        qkv = self.qkv(x)
        qkv = qkv.reshape(
            batch, length, 3, self.heads, self.head_width
        ).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)
        q, k, v = qkv.unbind(dim=0)
        scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(self.head_width)
        forbidden = torch.triu(
            torch.ones(length, length, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device),
            diagonal=1,
        )
        scores = scores.masked_fill(forbidden, float("-inf"))
        weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
        routed = weights @ v
        routed = routed.transpose(1, 2).reshape(batch, length, width)
        output = self.project(routed)
        if return_weights:
            return output, weights
        return output

## The Transformer block: residuals, normalization, and feedforward networks {#build-a-transformer-block}

Attention routes information across token positions. Transforming this mechanism into a
deep network requires two additional components: an unobstructed path through depth and
a nonlinear transformation at each position.

### The residual stream

@sec-09-modern-cnns-transfer introduced the residual stream: every sublayer reads from
the stream and writes an additive correction back. If a sublayer computes
$F(\vect{x})$, the residual update is

$$
\vect{x}\leftarrow \vect{x}+F(\vect{x}).
$$

The identity branch provides a direct conduit for representations and gradients, while
the learned branch proposes a local correction. This structure makes deep optimization
more tractable, though it does not eliminate the risk of vanishing or exploding
gradients.

Layer normalization controls feature scale along the representation axis. For a single
token vector $\vect{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$,

$$
\mu=\frac1d\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}x_\ell,\qquad \sigma^2=\frac1d\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}(x_\ell-\mu)^2,
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{LN}(\vect{x})_\ell =\gamma_\ell\frac{x_\ell-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}}+\beta_\ell,
\qquad \vect{\gamma},\vect{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^d.
$$

This adapts the normalization principle of @sec-09-modern-cnns-transfer to a different
tensor axis. Whereas `BatchNorm2d` pools statistics across batch and spatial dimensions
for each channel, LayerNorm operates along the feature axis of each token: it computes
empirical moments across the $d$ features within one token, without aggregating across
neighboring tokens or batch examples. Its formulation remains identical during training
and evaluation. Prior to applying the learned parameters $\vect{\gamma}$ and
$\vect{\beta}$, the normalized vector has mean zero and approximately unit variance.
<!-- print 2026-10-09, author-approved: LayerNorm's geometric reading, removing the projection onto the all-ones vector and rescaling to squared length just under d -->
Geometrically, subtracting $\mu$ removes $\mu(1,\ldots,1)$, the orthogonal projection of
$\vect{x}$ onto the all-ones vector. Dividing by $\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}$ scales the
squared Euclidean norm to $d\sigma^2/(\sigma^2+\epsilon)$. When $\sigma^2\gg\epsilon$,
this quantity approaches $d$, so the normalized token lies approximately on the sphere
of radius $\sqrt d$ within the zero-mean hyperplane.

Post-LayerNorm normalizes the aggregated representation after each residual addition,
analogous to applying an activation function after the shortcut merge in early ResNets
(@sec-09-modern-cnns-transfer). Pre-LayerNorm moves normalization into the function
branch, mirroring pre-activation ResNets. Pre-LayerNorm keeps an unobstructed identity
path along the residual stream, and in the experiments of
[Xiong et al.](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/xiong20b.html) it trained without the
learning-rate warmup (@sec-04-training-loss-sgd) that post-LayerNorm needed.

[**RMSNorm**](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/hash/1e8a19426224ca89e83cef47f1e7f53b-Abstract.html)
retains the rescaling but omits mean centering:

$$
\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\vect{x})
=\vect{g}\odot
\frac{\vect{x}}
{\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}x_\ell^2+\epsilon}}.
$$

It divides each token by its root-mean-square magnitude and applies a learned
per-feature gain $\vect{g}$.
<!-- print 2026-10-09, author-approved: RMSNorm rescales to length about sqrt(d) like LayerNorm but keeps the projection onto the all-ones vector -->
Prior to modulation by $\vect{g}$, it rescales $\vect{x}$ to a sphere of radius
approximately $\sqrt d$ without shifting the representation into the zero-mean subspace.
This omits one reduction operation per token. Whether this computational saving
translates into empirical gains depends on model scale, precision format, and memory
bandwidth.

### The position-wise feedforward network

Once tokens exchange information through attention, the same two-layer feedforward
network processes each sequence position independently:

$$
\operatorname{FFN}(\vect{z})
=\matr{W}_2\operatorname{ReLU}(\matr{W}_1\vect{z}+\vect{b}_1)+\vect{b}_2,
$$

where $\matr{W}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}\times d}$,
$\vect{b}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}}$, $\matr{W}_2\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times
d_{\text{ff}}}$, and $\vect{b}_2\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$.

With $\vect{w}_{1j}^\top$ as row $j$ of $\matr{W}_1$ and $\vect{u}_j$ as column $j$ of
$\matr{W}_2$, the transformation decomposes as

$$
\operatorname{FFN}(\vect{z})
=\sum_j [\vect{w}_{1j}^\top \vect{z}+b_{1j}]_+\,\vect{u}_j+\vect{b}_2.
$$

This decomposition highlights an interpretation of the feedforward network as a
key–value associative memory. Each row of $\matr{W}_1$ acts as a pattern detector, testing
whether the input falls within a learned half-space, and its rectified activation
determines the degree to which the value vector $\vect{u}_j$ is written to the
representation. While Transformer feedforward layers can exhibit associative-memory
behavior
empirically, this remains an operational analogy: the activations are unnormalized,
graded half-space responses rather than localized kernel weights that sum to one.

The complete block therefore alternates between two complementary operations:

1. causal multi-head attention routes information *between sequence positions*; and
2. the feedforward network transforms representations *within each individual
   position*.

Residual connections add the results of both operations to a single residual stream
that persists across the depth of the network.

<!-- print 2026-10-09, author-approved: box on what attention alone does to a stack of tokens (rank collapse, Dong, Cordonnier, and Loukas 2021), so residuals do an additional job in a Transformer: they keep the tokens distinct -->
::: {.callout-note}
## What attention alone does to a stack of tokens

Within each attention head, every output is a convex combination of that head's value
vectors, so it lies within their convex hull. The multi-head output concatenates these
averages and applies the output projection, a linear map that can move the result outside
the hull of the original value vectors. Without residual shortcuts or feedforward layers,
stacked attention layers apply such averaging again and again and can contract the token
representations toward a single shared representation.

[Dong, Cordonnier, and Loukas](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/dong21a.html)
formalized this rank collapse for unmasked attention. When the projection matrices are
small enough in norm and the token embeddings are clustered, the authors' bound on the
distance from the token matrix to a rank-one subspace shrinks doubly exponentially with
depth, with the exponent tripling at every layer. Their empirical evaluations reproduced
this collapse across pretrained language models when residual connections were removed.

The residual update $\vect{x}\leftarrow \vect{x}+F(\vect{x})$ provides a bypass around
every attention layer. The identity branch propagates token differences forward directly
without averaging, so the collapse is no longer forced. A shared position-wise FFN cannot
restore distinctions once token representations are identical. It maps identical inputs to
identical outputs. Feedforward layers can dilate existing token differences and slow the
collapse, and residual connections provide a path that bypasses the repeated averaging. The
cited collapse result holds under its stated assumptions. It does not describe every
attention architecture without residual connections.
:::

## From encoder–decoder translation to a causal language model {#from-the-original-transformer-to-this-experiment}

The original Transformer of [Vaswani et al.](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/hash/3f5ee243547dee91fbd053c1c4a845aa-Abstract.html) was an encoder–decoder architecture
designed for bilingual translation. Its encoder stack uses bidirectional (unmasked)
self-attention to construct contextual representations of the source sequence. Its
decoder stack applies causal self-attention over the target prefix, followed by
cross-attention whose queries originate in the decoder while keys and values are
retrieved from the encoder memory:

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\text{encoder:}& \matr{X}_s \to \text{self-attention} \to \text{FFN},\\
\text{decoder:}& \matr{X}_t \to \text{causal self-attention}
\to \text{cross-attention to encoder} \to \text{FFN}.
\end{array}
$$

The book-corpus task of @sec-10-sequences-rnn requires autoregressive next-character
prediction from preceding context alone. Because there is no external source sequence,
both the encoder stack and the cross-attention sublayers are unnecessary. The resulting
architecture is a **decoder-only causal Transformer** that consists of token and
positional embeddings, two pre-LayerNorm blocks, a final layer normalization, and a
linear projection to vocabulary logits. These logits feed directly into the
cross-entropy loss. Softmax normalization belongs inside attention routing and
autoregressive sampling, not between the output projection and the loss.

# [1]
def sinusoidal_positions(length: int, width: int) -> torch.Tensor:
    position = torch.arange(length, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)
    frequency = torch.exp(
        torch.arange(0, width, 2, dtype=torch.float32)
        * (-math.log(10_000.0) / width)
    )
    table = torch.zeros(length, width)
    table[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(position * frequency)
    table[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(position * frequency)
    return table

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(WIDTH)
        self.attention = CausalMultiHeadAttention(WIDTH, HEADS)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(WIDTH)
        self.ff = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(WIDTH, FF_WIDTH),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(FF_WIDTH, WIDTH),
        )

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, return_weights: bool = False):
        if return_weights:
            attended, weights = self.attention(self.norm1(x), True)
            x = x + attended
            return x + self.ff(self.norm2(x)), weights
        x = x + self.attention(self.norm1(x))
        return x + self.ff(self.norm2(x))

class TinyTransformerLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab: int, positions: bool) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.positions = positions
        self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab, WIDTH)
        nn.init.normal_(
            self.token_embedding.weight,
            mean=0.0,
            std=1 / math.sqrt(WIDTH),
        )
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(
            [TransformerBlock() for _ in range(BLOCKS)]
        )
        self.final_norm = nn.LayerNorm(WIDTH)
        self.output = nn.Linear(WIDTH, vocab)
        self.register_buffer(
            "position_table",
            sinusoidal_positions(CONTEXT, WIDTH),
            persistent=False,
        )

    def forward(self, tokens: torch.Tensor, return_weights: bool = False):
        length = tokens.shape[1]
        x = self.token_embedding(tokens) * math.sqrt(WIDTH)
        if self.positions:
            x = x + self.position_table[:length]
        maps = []
        for block in self.blocks:
            if return_weights:
                x, weights = block(x, True)
                maps.append(weights)
            else:
                x = block(x)
        logits = self.output(self.final_norm(x))
        return (logits, maps) if return_weights else logits

        ).item()
        tokens.append(next_token)
    return "".join(chars[index] for index in tokens)

of length $i+1$, allowing stacked layers to infer position from expanding receptive
fields. That is why the model without positional encodings performs better than an
orderless model would.

### Autoregressive sampling and qualitative evaluation {#listen-but-do-not-grade-by-fluency}

Both Transformer variants can generate text autoregressively: at each step, the model
truncates the context to the most recent 100 characters, evaluates a categorical
distribution over the vocabulary, samples a character, and appends it to the prefix.
Unlike the LSTM of @sec-10-sequences-rnn, this baseline implementation maintains no
persistent recurrent state. It evaluates the entire context window afresh at every
generation step.

## Practice bridge (optional): decoding is another model choice

For next-token logits $z_i$, **temperature** is the dial from @sec-02-logistic-softmax: it
divides each logit by $T$ before the softmax:

$$
p_i(T)=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_j\exp(z_j/T)},\qquad T>0.
$$

Lower $T$ concentrates probability; higher $T$ flattens it. **Top-$k$ sampling**
keeps the $k$ largest logits, sets the rest to negative infinity, then renormalizes.
[**Nucleus (top-$p$) sampling**](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751) first sorts the model probabilities and keeps the
smallest prefix whose cumulative mass reaches $p$, then renormalizes. The former fixes
a candidate count; the latter lets that count adapt to the distribution's shape.
Neither changes the trained weights, and neither guarantees a better sample.

This paragraph is approved on its own, while the surrounding NOVEL block still awaits sign-off -->
Keeping a set of tokens and renormalizing, as top-$k$ and nucleus sampling do, is what
the causal mask does to each attention row (zero the excluded entries, divide the rest
by their sum), with next tokens in place of keys. It gives the distribution over the
next token conditioned on that token lying in the kept set.
Enforcing a rule that forbids tokens, such as characters that would break the ISO date
format of @sec-11-encoder-decoder, conditions the distribution at each step in the same
way. A sampler that does this at every step need not return the outputs the rule allows
in proportion to their probabilities under the model
(Exercise 9 of @sec-11-encoder-decoder).

For evaluation, if $L$ is mean token negative log-likelihood in natural-log units,
**perplexity** is $\exp(L)$. It is an exponentiated loss, not a fluency score. Compare
it only under the same tokenization, data, and per-token averaging.

## Architectural trade-offs: gains and costs of self-attention {#what-the-architecture-bought}

During autoregressive generation, exact attention converts past context into both a
memory footprint and a computational bottleneck: every newly generated query must attend
over all preceding keys and values. A **key–value (KV) cache** stores the projected key
and value tensors from earlier steps, allowing new queries to attend over the prefix
without recomputing historical activations. In the nonparametric regression framework
of @sec-12-kernel-regression, the KV cache serves as the estimator's dataset: an
incoming query at step $t$ reads a table that grows with $t$, but earlier rows no longer
require recomputation. In contrast, our sampler re-evaluates a sliding 100-character
window with absolute slot encodings: when the window slides, every retained token shifts
to a new slot index, changing its input representation. Caching past the window limit
therefore requires a new positional or memory policy, not a drop-in speedup.
@sec-a3-precision-performance separates KV caching from FlashAttention's I/O-aware
kernel scheduling.

Self-attention leaves position and visibility to the modeler. @sec-15-bert-pretraining
modifies visibility itself, while @sec-16-vit-scaling explores what occurs when global
routing trades away an image model's locality bias.

Varying the kernel, predictor class, or update rule within this regression perspective
yields alternative memory formulations. The following interlude contrasts the growing KV
cache with finite sufficient statistics and delta updates.

Readers seeking deeper mathematical analysis of these architectures will find kernel
geometry, exact I/O-aware algorithms, parallel recurrence, and feature-learning regimes
in Shakeri (2026), [“Beyond This
Volume”](https://shakeri-lab.github.io/opt-book/chapters/beyond-this-volume.html#beyond).

## Okay, so: the Transformer routes, then transforms {#okay-so-the-transformer-routes-then-computes}

1. **Self-attention reuses the scaled dot-product operator within a single sequence.**
   Queries, keys, and values $\matr{Q},\matr{K},\matr{V}$ all derive from the same input
   $\matr{X}$, and one
   learned comparison rule is shared across every permitted query–key pair. All
   sequence positions can be evaluated in parallel during training, while
   autoregressive generation remains sequential.
2. **Without positional signals or a mask, self-attention is permutation
   equivariant, not invariant.**
   $\operatorname{SA}(\matr{P}\matr{X})=\matr{P}\operatorname{SA}(\matr{X})$. Sinusoidal
   clocks supply the order that
   global routing lacks (and that the convolutions of @sec-08-cnn built in), while
   sine–cosine coordinate pairs express relative displacements as planar rotations.
3. **Multi-head attention routes in parallel through partitioned subspaces.** The
   computation partitions $(B,n,d)\to(B,N_h,n,D_h)$, scales scores by $\sqrt{D_h}$, forms
   $(B,N_h,n,n)$ routing weights, concatenates, and projects. At fixed $d$, the four
   projection matrices hold $4d^2$ weights regardless of head count $N_h$.
4. **The causal mask defines visibility, not computational cost.** Future
   compatibility scores are set to $-\infty$ prior to softmax. The underlying operator
   remains quadratic in sequence length.
5. **The block alternates routing across positions and transformation within them.**
   The attention and feedforward sublayers both add corrections to the residual stream
   of @sec-09-modern-cnns-transfer, and layer normalization standardizes the features of
   each token independently.
6. **Position lowers held-out loss in this controlled benchmark.** Explicit positional
   encodings reduce held-out loss from 2.3405 to 1.9190. Under this matched protocol,
   the compact LSTM has a slightly lower held-out loss than the small Transformer
   (1.8881 versus 1.9190). An architecture changes inductive bias but does not
   guarantee lower loss in every scale and data regime.
